day-1.t: Day 1 — One shared sheet, not five copies

b.v: Today's goal

v: Create a sheet and share it with the right permission
Understand the three sharing levels in plain words
Set up your first shared fee register

b.v: About 20 minutes. A Google account is enough; nothing to install.

The biggest reason small offices lose track of money is five copies of the same file, each edited by a different person. One shared sheet removes that problem completely. Everyone types in the same place, at the same time, and you can see who changed what.
1) The three permissions

v: Viewer = can read only, good for a manager who reports but never types
Commenter = can leave notes but not change cells, good for review
Editor = can change anything, including formulas, so give it rarely

b.v: Most damage in shared sheets comes from editors, not from hackers. Give editor access to the two people who type, and viewer access to everyone else who only needs to look.
Share correctly:|Click Share in the top right|Type the email address of one person|Change the dropdown from Editor to Viewer|Untick Notify people if you do not want an email yet|Click Send
2) Build the register

Make one sheet called Fees with the columns below. Type the numbers exactly, then check the totals at the bottom against the ones I give you. Getting the arithmetic right on day one means every later lesson has a number you can trust.

v.cap: Sheet named Fees. Row 1 is the header. Balance is Fee Due minus Paid.

b.v: The sheet should show 20,400 due, 15,700 paid and 4,700 outstanding. Check by hand: 3,500 + 3,500 + 4,200 + 4,200 + 5,000 is 20,400, and 15,700 plus 4,700 is 20,400. If your row 7 does not show these three numbers, one of your typed values is wrong.
3) Use the version history

File, then Version history, then See version history. You can see every change, who made it, and restore an older version. This is your undo button for a whole morning of mistakes, and it is the reason shared sheets are safer than emailed files.
Never share a sheet as Anyone with the link can edit. That link gets forwarded on WhatsApp and your fee register becomes public. Share with named people only.
Practice

Create the Fees sheet exactly as shown and confirm the three totals. Share it with one person as Viewer. Then open Version history and name the current version Starting point, so you can return to it later.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Formulas that copy down without breaking

b.v: Today's goal

v: Tell relative from absolute references using the dollar sign
Fix the classic drag-down error
Wrap formulas in IFERROR so errors do not spread

b.v: About 20 minutes. Type formulas by hand; do not copy from this page.
A formula is a small instruction that starts with an equals sign. The hard part is not the maths; it is understanding what happens to the cell addresses when you copy the formula down a hundred rows.
1) Relative and absolute

v: A2 = relative, so it moves when the formula is copied
$A$2 = absolute, so it stays on the same cell
A$2 = the row is locked, the column moves
$A2 = the column is locked, the row moves

b.v: If every student pays the same monthly fee, put that fee in one cell and lock it. Here the monthly fee is 3,500 in cell H1, so a formula of C2*$H$1 works for every row.

v.cap: A small fee table with one locked rate. H1 is the monthly rate.

b.v: Ali pays 3,500 for one month, Ayesha 7,000 for two, and Hina 10,500 for three. The dollar signs in $H$1 are what make the copied formula keep pointing at the rate cell instead of sliding down to an empty row.
2) The drag-down mistake

Write a formula without dollar signs where you needed them and every copied row points one cell lower than it should. The totals look plausible, which is why nobody notices. Always test the last row by clicking it and reading the formula bar.

Check a copied formula:|Click the last cell in the column|Look at the formula bar and confirm the references make sense|Press Ctrl and the grave accent key to show all formulas at once|Press it again to go back to values
3) Stop errors spreading
A single #DIV/0! or #N/A makes a whole summary look broken, and a VLOOKUP that fails fills a column with errors. IFERROR replaces the error with something calm, such as a zero or a blank.
Do not wrap a formula in IFERROR until you know what the error was. Hiding a broken lookup hides a wrong price, and a wrong price reaches the customer.
Practice
Add a monthly rate of 3,500 in cell H1 and a Total column using =B2*$H$1. Copy it down all five rows. Change H1 to 4,000 and confirm every total updates. Then restore 3,500.

day-3.t: Day 3 — ARRAYFORMULA: one formula for a whole column

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write one formula that fills an entire column
Make it skip empty rows cleanly
Know when not to use it

b.v: About 20 minutes. Delete the Balance column formulas from Day 1 first.

Dragging a formula down works until row 400, then you add row 401 and forget. ARRAYFORMULA solves the whole column at once and keeps working as new rows arrive. It is the single best habit in Google Sheets.
1) The pattern
Instead of one cell, point at a whole range. Put nothing below it, because an array formula needs the empty cells underneath to write its answers into.

@Formula
=ARRAYFORMULA(C2:C6 - D2:D6)

v.cap: One formula in D2 fills all five rows of Balance. Nothing is typed below it.

b.v: The five answers that appear in D2 to D6 are 0, 1500, 0, 3200 and 0. Check one by hand: Hina's fee is 4,200 and she paid 1,000, so 3,200 is right. Because one formula produced all five answers, there is no chance of a single row being different from the rest.
2) Skip empty rows
An array formula applied to 1,000 rows shows a zero or a strange value on all the empty ones. Wrap it in IF so blank rows stay blank. This is the version you should use in a real sheet.

@Formula
=ARRAYFORMULA(IF(B2:B = "", "", B2:B - C2:C))
3) When it is the wrong tool

v: When each row needs a different rule, a normal formula is clearer
When someone else will edit the sheet and does not know arrays, add a note
When the range includes a total row, because the total gets counted twice

b.v: Keep your total row outside the array range. If the array covers B2:B, and the total sits in B10, the array will overwrite it or double count it. Put totals in a different column or a different block.
If you see #REF! after adding an array formula, the cells below are not empty. Clear them, then paste the formula again.
Practice

Clear the Balance column and replace it with one ARRAYFORMULA in E2 that hides blanks. Add a sixth student row and type a fee of 4,200 with 2,100 paid. The balance 2,100 must appear by itself, and your totals must update without you touching anything.

day-4.t: Day 4 — QUERY basics: SQL inside a sheet

b.v: Today's goal

v: Read a QUERY formula without fear
Select only the columns and rows you need
Sort, filter and total with one formula

b.v: About 22 minutes. Keep the Fees sheet open.
QUERY asks a question of your data using a small language that looks like SQL. You do not need to learn SQL to use it — you need four patterns, and you will have them by the end of this lesson.
1) The shape of the formula
Three parts: the data range, the question in quotes, and the number of header rows. The question uses column letters A, B, C of the range, not your sheet's real letters.

@Formula
=QUERY(Fees!A1:E6, "select A, C, D, E", 1)

v: select = which columns to return
where = which rows to keep
order by = how to sort
sum, count, avg = totals
label = rename an output column

b.v: 2) Filter and sort
This returns only students who still owe money, biggest debt first: Hina Riaz with 3,200 and Ayesha Khan with 1,500.

@Formula
=QUERY(Fees!A1:E6, "select A, E where E > 0 order by E desc", 1)

v.cap: The output of the query above

b.v: 3) Totals without a SUM cell
QUERY can total for you. This returns 15,700, the amount collected, and 4,700, the amount still owed. No helper column, no total row to forget.

The second line groups by class: class 5 collected 5,500, class 6 collected 5,200, class 7 collected 5,000. Those three add to 15,700, which matches the first line. If they do not match, your range is missing a row.
Never point QUERY at a range that contains its own output. The output is data too, so the query reads itself and doubles. Put the query on a separate sheet or far to the right.
Practice
On a new sheet called Report, write three queries: everyone who paid in full, the two biggest balances sorted, and the total collected per class. Check that the three class totals add to 15,700.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Data validation: stop bad data at the door

b.v: Today's goal

v: Add dropdown lists so people cannot invent spellings
Limit numbers to a sensible range
Show a helpful error message instead of a red box

b.v: About 20 minutes. This is the cheapest quality control in any shared sheet.
Bad data is much harder to clean than to prevent. Lahore, lahore, Lhr and Lahore (with a space) are four different cities to a formula. A dropdown makes them one.
1) A dropdown from a list
Data, then Data validation, then Add rule. Choose Dropdown and type the options. Tick Show dropdown list in cell and reject the input if it does not match.

Add a city dropdown:|Select the City column, rows 2 to 500|Data, then Data validation, then Add rule|Criteria: Dropdown, and type Lahore, Karachi, Multan, Islamabad|On invalid data: Reject the input|Appearance: show a warning text such as Choose a city from the list
2) Numbers with limits
A fee cannot be negative and is unlikely to be above 50,000 in a small school. A number rule catches a typed 35000 that was meant to be 3500 — one extra zero, a whole month of confusion.

v: Number between = a minimum and a maximum
Number greater than = only a minimum, useful for quantities
Text contains = a soft check, hard to enforce strictly
Custom formula = any rule you can write, such as must be a weekday

v.cap: A validation rule written as a custom formula. This one allows only dates in the current month.

b.v: 3) Helpful messages
An error that says Invalid input teaches nobody. An error that says Enter the amount received in rupees, for example 3500 teaches the person and reduces the messages you get on WhatsApp at night.
Validation does not fix data that is already there. Apply the rule, then look down the column for existing wrong entries, or the rule will sit quietly on bad data.
Practice

Add a city dropdown to a new City column in your Fees sheet, and a number rule on Paid between 0 and 100,000 with a clear error message. Test both by typing Lhr and by typing -500, and confirm both are refused.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Protect the formulas, not the people

b.v: Today's goal

v: Protect a range so only you can edit it
Leave input cells open for the team
Use named ranges to make formulas readable

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this on the shared Fees sheet.
Someone types over a formula once and the totals are wrong for a month. Protecting the formula column, while leaving the input columns free, removes that risk without slowing anybody down.
1) Protect a sheet or a range

Data, then Protect sheets and ranges. You can protect a whole sheet or just selected cells, and you can choose who is allowed to edit. Set it to yourself plus one backup person, so the file is never locked out.
Protect the totals column:|Select E1 to E200|Data, then Protect sheets and ranges|Name it Balance column|Set permissions to Only you, plus one other editor|Click Done and test by trying to type in E3

v: Protected range = cells nobody can edit except the listed people
Warning only = shows a message but still allows the change, good for soft rules
Sheet protection = the whole tab, use it for a report sheet

b.v: 2) Named ranges
Data, then Named ranges gives a block of cells a word. =SUM(Collected) is easier to check than =SUM(D2:D400), especially for the person who takes over from you.

v.cap: Three named ranges on the Fees sheet

b.v: 3) Tell people what is protected
A protected cell that silently refuses an edit feels like a broken sheet. Add a note in row 1 or a comment on the header: grey columns are automatic, please type only in white columns.
Protection is not security. Anyone with edit access can copy the sheet and change the copy. Protect against accidents, and keep truly private data in a different file with viewer-only access.
Practice

Create the three named ranges, protect the Balance column, and add a header note explaining which columns to type in. Then try to edit a protected cell to confirm the protection is working, and unprotect one cell to prove you can.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Google Forms straight into a sheet

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a short form that people fill on their phone
Send responses into your sheet automatically
Keep the raw responses separate from your working sheet

b.v: About 22 minutes. You need a Google account and a phone to test the form.
Typing from WhatsApp messages into a sheet is slow and full of mistakes. A form puts the typing on the other person's phone, in the shape you chose, and the answers land in a sheet as a clean row.
1) Keep the form short
Five questions maximum. Every question should be a dropdown, a number or a short text — never a long paragraph that you will have to read and retype later. Ask for the minimum you need to act.

v: Short answer = free text, use it as little as possible
Multiple choice = one of a fixed list, good for a city or a class
Number = only digits accepted, good for an amount
Required = the form will not submit without it

b.v: 2) Link it to a sheet

In the form, open the Responses tab and click Link to Sheets, then Create a new spreadsheet. Every submission appears as a new row with a timestamp. Never type in that tab — treat it as the raw record.

Set up the response sheet:|Create the form with five questions|Responses tab, then Link to Sheets, then Create a new spreadsheet|Open the new sheet and rename the tab Raw|Add a second tab called Working and copy the header row there|Do your formulas on the Working tab, reading from Raw

v.cap: How the response sheet looks after two submissions

b.v: 3) Read it with QUERY
On the Working tab, pull only what you need from the raw rows. This query totals the money received by payment method, which is exactly the kind of question a shop owner asks at month end.

@Formula
=QUERY(Raw!A1:E, "select E, sum(D) group by E label sum(D) 'Received'", 1)
If you delete or sort rows on the Raw tab, the form's own records get confused. Leave Raw alone and work on a copy. Sorting raw responses by hand also breaks the timestamp order you may need later.
Practice

Build a five-question fee payment form. Submit it twice from your phone, once as JazzCash and once as Easypaisa. Confirm both rows appear on the Raw tab with timestamps, then run the QUERY above on a Working tab and check the two totals.

day-8.t: Day 8 — IMPORTRANGE and one report from many files

b.v: Today's goal

v: Pull data from another spreadsheet with IMPORTRANGE
Fix the #REF! permission error properly
Build a small summary file that reads three branch files

b.v: About 20 minutes. You need at least two spreadsheets.

Many small offices keep one file per branch, then retype the numbers into a master file every month. IMPORTRANGE removes the retyping entirely. The master reads the branch files live, so it can never be out of date.
1) The formula
Two parts: the spreadsheet address in quotes, and the tab and range in quotes, separated by a comma. The tab name comes first, then an exclamation mark, then the cells.

@Formula
=IMPORTRANGE("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/PASTE_THE_ID_HERE/edit", "Fees!A1:E100")

v: URL = the full address of the other spreadsheet
Range = TabName!A1:D50, with the tab name spelled exactly
First-time approval = a one-off click that allows the connection

b.v: 2) The #REF! error

The first time you use it you will see #REF! until you hover over the cell and click Allow access. This is a permission step, not a broken formula. The person who owns the source file must also share it with you.

Connect two files:|Open the master file and click a cell|Paste the IMPORTRANGE formula with the source address|Hover the cell and click Allow access|If it still fails, ask the owner to share the source as Viewer|Check that the first row is the header you expected

v.cap: A master file reading three branches, each with its own row

b.v: 3) Keep it small
Import the smallest range you need, not a whole sheet of a thousand rows. IMPORTRANGE can be slow, and a heavy file makes everyone's browser struggle — especially on a phone with a weak connection.
IMPORTRANGE needs both files to stay in place. If someone moves the source file to the bin or renames the tab, your master file breaks with #REF! and every number in it disappears.
Practice

Create two small spreadsheets called branch-lahore and branch-karachi, each with a Summary tab holding collected and outstanding amounts. Build a master file that imports both, then add a total row and check it equals the sum of the two.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Your first Apps Script that does real work

b.v: Today's goal

v: Open the script editor and run one line of JavaScript
Write a script that marks every student who still owes money
Set a trigger so it runs without you

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the lesson where the sheet starts working for you.
Apps Script is JavaScript that can read and write your spreadsheet. Twenty lines can replace twenty minutes of copying every Monday morning. Start with one small job, get it working, then grow it.
1) The pieces

v: Extensions, then Apps Script = opens the editor
function = a named block of instructions
SpreadsheetApp = the object that talks to your sheet
Logger.log = prints a message so you can see what happened

b.v: Before touching the sheet, try the logic in plain JavaScript. The code below is exactly the loop the script will run, and you can run it right here.

You should see two reminders, for Ayesha Khan at 1,500 and Hina Riaz at 3,200, and an outstanding total of 4,700. That matches the sheet from Day 1, which is how you know the logic is right before you connect it to real data.
2) The same thing on the real sheet
Row 1 is the header, so the loop starts at row 2. Column E is the balance and column F is where we write the note. getRange row and column numbers start at 1, not 0.

Run it once:|In the editor, paste the function and press Ctrl+S|Choose markReminders from the dropdown and press Run|Approve the permission prompt the first time|Go back to the sheet and look at column F|Fix the header in F1 to say Status
3) A trigger, so you never press Run again

In the editor, the clock icon opens Triggers. Add a trigger for markReminders, time-driven, daily. Now the sheet updates itself. Keep an eye on the executions list for the first week in case something fails.
Never put a password or an API key in a script. Anyone who opens the script editor with edit access can read it, and a sheet shared too widely leaks it further.
Practice

Run the JavaScript version in the page and read the output. Then paste the Apps Script version, run it on your Fees sheet, and confirm column F says Reminder needed for Ayesha and Hina only. Finally, add a daily trigger and check the execution list the next day.

day-10.t: Day 10 — A monthly report that builds itself

b.v: Today's goal

v: Combine QUERY, IMPORTRANGE and a script into one small system
Write a one-page guide so anyone can take over
Decide what should not be automated

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the finishing lesson, so test everything twice.

Automation is only useful if you can trust it and hand it over. A sheet that quietly emails wrong numbers is worse than a sheet that needs ten minutes of typing, because nobody checks the automatic one.
1) The monthly pack
Three tabs do the whole job. Raw holds form responses, Working holds clean formulas, Summary holds three numbers and one chart. Nothing else is needed, and every tab has one clear owner.

v.cap: The Summary tab. Three numbers, no clutter, checked against the source.

b.v: The collection rate is 15,700 divided by 20,400, which is about 0.77, or 77 percent. If the rate and the two amounts disagree, one of the three numbers is reading a different range.
2) Test like a stranger
Add one fake payment, refresh, and see whether all four numbers move correctly. Then delete the fake row and confirm the numbers return. A system you have only seen work once is not tested.

v: Add a test row and check every number changes as expected
Delete the test row and check the numbers return exactly
Open the file on a phone, which is where most readers will see it
Ask one other person to run it from the written guide, without your help

b.v: 3) What not to automate

Do not automate anything that decides money, such as marking a fee as paid, without a human check. Do not automate a formula you do not understand. And never automate sending a message to a customer before you have read the message yourself a few times.
Every automation needs a named owner and a monthly look. A script nobody owns keeps running with yesterday's assumptions, and the first person to notice is usually a customer with a wrong bill.
Practice

Build the three-tab pack with the four summary numbers. Add a test payment, confirm every number moves, then remove it and confirm the numbers return. Write a one-page guide with the tabs, the owner of each, how to add a month, and who to call. Then give the guide to someone else and watch them use it without your help.
